RETZLAW, alias GROEHL.

Yesterday M-D asked me if I knew anything about this man. He told me that Retzlau had called on Opuchensky, of the Czech Foreign Office, and given him a copy of his manifesto. He told him that he was a former police president of Munich. Opuchensky asked M.D. whether this was true. M.D. replied that to the best of his knowledge it was not true because (1) He knew all the names of these functionaries in Munich for a long time back and (2) he had known Retzlau in Germany as a communist whose activities were centred round Berlin. He made the reservation, however, that Retzlau might have held this office for a very brief period during the Soviet regime set up in Munich in 1919. M.D. then asked Vogel whether he thought there was any possibility that Retzlau had ever been police president of Munich. Vogel thought not, but said he would check up and let M.D. know later, giving it as his opinion that Retzlau was a swindler.

Retzlau also informed Opuchensky that he was at present working for the War Office.

M.D. thinks Retzlau may have another name, but does not know it.

Later in the day I asked Otten what Groehl was doing and how he was getting on. (Otten does not know that I am aware of the alias) He told me Groehl was suffering from ill health and therefore "not so efficient as we should like him to be." He added that Groehl was very credulous and also very obstinate; when he had made up his mind on a certain point, he was impervious to reason and apt to lose his temper with anyone who tried to argue him out of a preconceived opinion. He described him as a born conspirator who was spoiling his chances of doing something useful by his foolish behaviour. He hated the German Socialist movement because he was only too conscious of its shortcomings during the Weimar period, but Otten said that was no excuse for him writing his manifesto and distributing it to all and sundry. In fact he was doing a lot of harm that way.

I rather gathered from Otten's tone that the two men must have quarrelled; also it would seem that he is making himself far too conspicuous at present.

C.W. Sykes.
S.3. 16/1/42
